utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we begin as usual by taking today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner; and this morning, a new face, Charlotte Frew, who's temporarily attached to our team, is with me, and I don't think Your Honour can see, but she is behind me; together, as always, with Crispian Smith, case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cukic for the Zupljanin Defence. Mr. Zupljanin is not present; he already signed a waiver. Thank you. Mr. Zupljanin is not present. He already signed a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, could the -- I assume the usher has gone to escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic. I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, during the night I looked at the transcript, and there are a couple of things that I need to address. Something needs to be changed in the transcript. Now, since you and I overlapped when speaking, it is no surprise that the transcript needs to be corrected here and there and that there might have been some slips by the interpreters. On page 9627, for instance, line 6, when you were talking about Mr. Hasan Cengic. It says here that he wanted to introduce a pro-Iranian, pro-Shiite elements in the work of his party, aspects in the work of his party, and I think you said that he wanted to do that in the state rather than the party. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that, I asked you about Bosnia and Herzegovina and what it was like, what kind of state it was like before the 1992 events, compared to its secular character, if you recall, and I don't think that part of your answer was recorded. I believe you said or, rather, confirmed when I asked you that it was a secular state, and that since that you were born in Herzegovina yourself, that you call the Muslims in Herzegovina Turks, because -- let me put it this way, because of the 500-year presence of the Turkish Ottoman empire in that area. And since Turkey is a secular state, that is to say, the state is separate from the church and religion or, rather, religion, you used that example to show what Bosnia and Herzegovina was like. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said how nice it was to live there, to live in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now the crux of the matter is that the situation started to change with the arrival of, let me say, the radical Islamists to power.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the arrival of the radical Islamists in the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action in fact. And through them, it was these pro-Iranian, pro-Shiite people that came into power who tried to introduce religious laws into state institutions and organs, and that was where the problem lay. And that, of course, started in the police force with the arrival of Mirsad Srebrenkovic. And he was a religious teacher in the great mosque in Zagreb in Croatia, which is where he is today, and where he is working to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now for the transcript, Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic has joined the Defence team for Mico Stanisic today. Now on page 9634 of the transcript, line 1, the first line, when you were speaking about -- well, my question to you was about the fact that we had information telling us that some people who had criminal files were employed in the police force, and you confirmed that. And then you gave us an example with respect to the fact that the former Yugoslavia still existed, so it was possible for you to establish -- to access criminal files from other republics.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your full answer was not recorded in the transcript, because if I remember correctly, what you said was, That's how we entered and accessed the information centre and established the fact that such and such person had a criminal report in Sandzak in Serbia, and that they were nonetheless employed in the MUP of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was absolutely against all the rules, to employ someone with a criminal police file; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And especially people from other states in the police.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was one state, a single state. Bosnia-Herzegovina was, at the time, a component part of Yugoslavia, so that wasn't a problem. However, in the meantime of course, Slovenia, Macedonia, and Croatia proclaimed independence, and they were already foreign citizens, while the citizens of Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Montenegro still lived in a single state, and the political leadership of those republics, in 1991 at least, recognised it as being one state which was, of course, Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next intervention I'd like to make to the transcript is 9642, page 9642, line 21. I'm sure you'll remember the document we were looking at of the Serbian Democratic Party which referred to a Presidency meeting of the 2nd of March, and you said that it was most probably a mistake in the typing, a typo. And then you said: "I can remember the sequence of events." And in the transcript what was record was that you could not remember the sequence of events. So your answer was, I can remember in the affirmative?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I explained how that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now my last intervention to the transcript is on page 9643, line 11, and I'm sure you'll recall that same document, and we were discussing the very end of the document, where it refers to Munir Alibabic, and you explained to us about Munir Alibabic. However, on that same page, 9643, line 11, as I've already quoted, it was not recorded the way you put it, to the best of my recollections. What you said was this, you said that Mr. Munir Alibabic mixed up different conversations or, rather, edited them and transferred them from cassettes to tapes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we were told by one of his operatives in one of the cases before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I said that at the proposal of the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal, Carla Del Ponte, proceedings were taken against him, and the High Commissioner for Bosnia-Herzegovina forbade him to deal in police affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that one of his operatives explained to the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, explained this, do you mean he explained the way in which Munir Alibabic transferred the intercepts, telephone-intercepted conversations, and made a collage of them and made them into one whole?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he explained the ways and means of doing this and how people dealt with these intercepts, the way in which one could go about that and did go about that. So the operative explained how you could mix and join them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Very well. Let's continue where we left off yesterday then. Now, in addition to the situation that we explained, and we've reached February 1992, I believe, there were a series of other contentious issues which cropped up on a daily basis in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, for instance, that there was one particular problem between the public security station at Pale, where the chief was Mr. Malko Koroman, and the public security station Stari Grad, in Sarajevo, where the chief was a certain manned named, Ismet Dahic. And these two public security stations bordered on each other. They were neighbouring stations on the territory of Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the questions, thank you; just the answers, please. If I remember rightly, you said that you were in charge of dealing with the problem that occurred between these two public security stations, and the problem was as follows: This man, Ismet Dahic, the chief of the Stari Grad police station, let go all the ethnic Serbs from the public security station. He dismissed them and did not want, despite an order received from the Ministry of the Interior, and the minister himself, to appoint a commander, a komandir, who was a Serb in the public security station. And you, I believe, if I remember correctly, were given the assignment of implementing that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now as retribution that conduct on the part of Ismet Dahic -- Malko Koroman for his part from the Pale public security station also refused to follow the order from the MUP and the minister to appoint a commander, junior commander, komandir, who was a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you tried or -- rather, you were given the assignment to resolve the problem, and as far as I remember, you were not successful; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Pale municipality and Stari Grad municipality in Sarajevo are neighbouring municipalities. Pale has a Serb majority, and Stari Grad has a Muslim majority. Now, the top people in the police force belonged to the ethnicity that was in the majority, so Pale had a Serb; Stari Grad had a Muslim; and vice versa. Now the number two man, in ethnic terms, were the ethnicity of the number two majority. Now Dahic, who was a cadet together with me at the Military Academy, refused to receive as commander a man called Milosevic, somebody who had been working in the police force for many years, and he didn't let him perform his functions. And at the time he raised 6.000 reserve policemen, I believe. 600 reserve policemen. Now, the -- it boomeranged, and there was a physical settling of cuffs between myself and Malko Koroman, who didn't understand the importance of the order and had to do that. And as a Serb cadre myself, I tried to explain the situation to him and told him that he couldn't be stubborn on that point and couldn't base his actions on what people were doing in another municipality because then it would be a chain reaction all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. And who know what the consequences of that would have been. But I wasn't able to persuade him, Dahic or the other man. And so the commanders were never -- at Pale was never a Muslim, or in Stari Grad was there a Serb. And it's the place where the wedding party with -- displaying the Serbian flag and the man from the wedding party was killed, that is the same Stari Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you misspoke. You said Ismet Dahic, that he was your -- I think you made a slip of the tongue. That he was at the Military Academy.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I meant to say the police academy. We were in the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm sure you'll agree with me that that situation reflected the fact that the authority of the Ministry of the Interior, even in Sarajevo itself, where it had its seat, was not sufficiently strong to impose its orders on the chiefs of the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about the autumn 1991 and the arrival of Denkovic [phoen]. Now the authority of this ministry as a homogenous entity began to be disrupted, and this had a ripple effect. When this man from Croatia came to head it, this was, of course, reflected on the individual environments, which accepted or did not accept the way in which he worked. So that's the example of Stari Grad municipality and Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So we agree that the crux of the problem was that the Ministry of Interior's authority in the autumn of 1991 compared to its territorial branches, and I mean the Security Services Centres, the public security stations, was significantly disrupted; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we have a saying by which we say that the fish stinks from the head, not the tail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now let's summarise the situation. From the autumn of 1991, the situation in the Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you have told us, drastically deteriorated, the crisis became deeper.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there was general mistrust amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now you, and when I say "you," I mean the collegium, the leaders, especially the Serb leaders - tried to resolve the problem within the Ministry of the Interior. And yesterday you confirmed and said that you attended a number of meetings with the minister but that the minister told that you that he himself was incapable and -- of resolving the situation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I and my close associates are concerned, both Muslim, Serbs, and Croats, we tried to solve the situation in our own house first. And we held a number of meetings in that regard. And after that, we organised meetings of Serb cadres both in Sarajevo, and I think in Banja Luka too, to discuss those problems, and then we would report back to the Minister Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to that in due course. Now we're going to speak about the second half of 1991. So after you held the meetings and tried to resolve that within your own house first, after that, you wrote a letter to the Presidency and the government and the Presidential Commission for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, that is to say, all the relevant institutions, you wrote to all of them and pointed out the irregularities and unlawfulness of the work of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that was my duty. All I was doing was doing my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, due to the fact that your letters did not bear fruit, letters to the top state institutions did not bring about any results, you, as we saw, addressed the public in September and then again in February and so on and so forth. And in your addresses to the public, you were joined by the Serbian Democratic Party, or, Dr. Karadzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic liked to meddle in these cadre problems. He always wanted to have a finger in the pie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you'll agree that addressing the public and presenting the problems publicly and indicating the seriousness of those problems had, as its goal -- well, that was your last chance, to resolve the problem under pressure from the public.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we couldn't solve the problem in our own home and couldn't resolve the problem by appealing to the Serb cadres and holding meetings, then all that was left to us to do was to inform the public, so that the public should be informed about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, none of that resulted in anything concrete.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And parallel to what was going on in the Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a serious political process under way at the time. That is to say, in the autumn of 1991. And then in October, completely unconstitutionally, in the Assembly, a declaration was proclaimed on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think with the deterioration of the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, that was helped by the war in Croatia, I think, because the Bosnian Croats did all they could to make life difficult for Serbs in BH as a consequence of the war in Croatia. And that part of the Muslim leadership wanted to have its own state. This is to say, they wanted to have Islamic and religious laws introduced into state organisations. So in that general Bosnian pot, cauldron, there were problems, disagreements, and then we saw the spring and the war follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that unconstitutional or, rather, less violent act against the constitution when this declaration of independence was adopted unconstitutionally, after that, in December, the Presidency and the cabinet decided, again without participation of the Serb representatives in those bodies, to request the recognition of the -- of the independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Plavsic and Dr. Koljevic withdrew from their positions in the Presidency, so what was left was a so-called truncated Presidency which consisted of the representatives of the Muslim people and Mr. Ejub Ganic who declared himself to be a Yugoslav. But he is now standing trial in the United Kingdom because he plays a role in the attack on the column withdrawing from Sarajevo where many people came to harm, including children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a public broadcast, and I do think that it is only right, particularly as these are ongoing proceedings, I think it should be made absolutely clear that Mr. Ganic is not standing trial for anything in the United Kingdom. Serbia has made a request for his extradition. He is awaiting extradition. The United Kingdom is not trying him for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly, Ms. Korner, what the witness said; it was only recorded wrongly in the transcript. I wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, sir, that Ejub Ganic was in London and that Serbia requested his extradition to carry out a procedure because of the killing of the children in the Dobrovojacka Street?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I didn't say that he was being tried in England. He only mentioned the extradition proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So as a result of this declaration of independence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a result of this declaration which was adopted in an unconstitutional manner in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs established the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They walked out from the joint parliament and established the Assembly of the Serb people. So the same members of parliament who had been elected at the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who belonged to the Serb people walked out and established the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That establishment of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the separation of Serb members of parliament, is a direct result of this constitutional violence in October 1991 and the unconstitutional adoption of the declaration of independence.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was actually a -- a down-voting or majoritisation of the Serb members of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your question -- answer to my question is affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tend to add things to explain them better. But I can be briefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that, as we saw in December, that incomplete Presidency without Serb representatives and a cabinet requested the recognition of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the international community.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The result of that move of the Muslim and Croat peoples, or, rather, their representatives, is the creation of the RS in January 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After the creation of the RS, and all the events that we know about, the international community and the European Union, especially the latter, started a process that is known under the popular name of the Cutileiro Plan. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jose Cutileiro, a Portuguese diplomate, represented the European Community or the internation community and he had some suggestions as to the structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the future as an independent state. That plan was adopted by Croats, Muslims, and Serbs at a certain moment, and the Sarajevo Agreement was signed in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, very briefly, if we can see 1D133. And let us very briefly comment on the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 1D133. 133.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is a document with a heading: Statement on the principles of new constitutional arrangements for Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the document that you were talking about and to which all ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed. It was drafted by the European Union, and it is popularly called the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In item 1 it says that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be an independent state composed of three constituent units. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this plan almost by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you know that the plan foresees that each constituent unit have its own police; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was to reflect the ethnic structure of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the witness 1D01-0936. [In English] 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, this document is basically a document with which the Croatian democratic Union agrees to the Cutileiro Plan, and it was published in the Zagreb daily "Vjesnik" on 26 February 1992. We see that in the lower left corner. And we see that under paragraph B it says that the HDZ accepted this proposal without objections. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this correspond to your recollection that the Croats accepted the Cutileiro Plan as something acceptable to the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are objections, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] First, Your Honour, we really cannot have a two-fold thing. Either newspaper articles go in without objection from other side subject to relevance, or the same rules apply. The second matter is this. I don't know what this is. There is only a partial page of it. And I see it's -- is that "Kozarski Vjesnik"? Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the footnote we can see that the source is "Vjesnik." At the time, it was the number one daily in Croatia. It's called "Vjesnik," and it was published in Zagreb. I don't know whether it is still published.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But there is a publication called "Kozarski Vjesnik" as well. Is that different?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the fact remains, I would like to see the full article. I have no objection, subject to the -- and a full translation, obviously. Otherwise, but as I say, there's got to be one rule for both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, may I inquire, first of all, Mr. Zecevic, is this a newspaper comment on the Cutileiro Plan, or is it the Cutileiro Plan as published by the newspaper in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is my understanding, Your Honours, that this is the -- the proclamation of the Croatian Democratic Union, the party of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is referring to their position on the Cutileiro Plan, which was published by this "Vjesnik" from Zagreb newspaper. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The reason why I was asking is whether the -- there wouldn't exist some more authoritative source than having to rely on a newspaper -- newspaper account, as it were. But, Ms. Korner, you were about to say something on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the moment, Your Honour, all I'm asking for is the full article, please, and not just one page from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you know our position with regard to newspaper articles. I'm not sure now, but I think that this document -- and you may remember four to five months ago Mr. Tom Hannis disclosed to us a certain number of documents that have to do with the Cutileiro Plan. At this moment, I really cannot say whether this document is part of that. Therefore, my submission would be to mark this document for identification, so as not to waste time now so I might proceed. This could be the best solution. And in the meantime we can try to find the original documents to support our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it even meets the threshold as set out for marking for identification. It is a partial part of a newspaper report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since Ms. Korner opposes, I will withdraw my submission and continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously you're going to return to this at some point, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, Mr. Mandic, isn't it, that the Serbian side very firmly backed up the Cutileiro Plan and supported it as an absolutely acceptable solution for a peaceful transition of Bosnia-Herzegovina into a new situation which would be an independent state with three entities; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all three ruling parties supported the Cutileiro Plan, at least initially, and signed it. And when it should have been ratified in the parliament, Alija Izetbegovic gave up the plan, and then when he was asked about it, he uttered that famous sentence. He was asked, Why do you give up -- why did you give up the plan, Mr. President? He answered, I have one opinion in the morning and another in the afternoon. The Croats didn't give up, only -- or didn't back out. Only the representatives of the Muslim people did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: His refusal of the plan was in late March 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, that is to say, in late January and all through February while the parties were fine-tuning the Cutileiro Plan and they all stated their acceptance, that is the end of January, all of February, and a major part of March; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, on the 11th of February, a meeting was held in Banja Luka, which is 1D135. You spoke about it a short while ago, saying that the Serb personnel got together to speak about the problems in the MUP of the socialist republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they had became unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this was the second meeting of Serb staff about these problems. The first one took place in Sarajevo and the second in Banja Luka. The one in Banja Luka was held at the Bosna hotel, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the meeting in Banja Luka wasn't a secret meeting by any means, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally informed Mr. Delimustafic of that meeting. I believe that even a copy of the minutes was -- was sent to the minister. We wanted to acquaint him with our conclusions. There was no reason for it to be secret. I believe that I informed him by phone and maybe even in a dispatch about the time and place of the meeting. There was no reason for it to be secret. We were desperately -- we were making a desperate appeal to regulate things to put them into order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can show you page 2 of these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please. In the Serbian. The English page is correct. Page 2, please. Madam, page 2 in the Serbian, not in the English. The English version had the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we have Mico Stanisic address those in attendance. He said that the minimum requests pending need to be assembled and sent to the minister, Mr. Delimustafic, with a set deadline. This is precisely what you were saying when you said that you forwarded it to Mr. Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We asked that policemen not be fired because they were Serbs and that no personnel be employed on the Muslim side without previous checks and that there should be a balance and that the Law on Internal Affairs and the rules of service should be observed. It was nothing out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One of the conclusions in item 19 is something I wanted to read out to you, and perhaps can you confirm to me whether you recall it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to repeat -- well, there's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that your wish was to have your positions made public from the meeting concerning the irregularities which were taking place at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, there's an opinion expressed here that that meeting was intentionally held in the Bosna hotel in Banja Luka so as to hold it covertly. What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we wanted to do it in secret, we would have used a police building or a state building without the presence of the public. We had waiters waiting on us in the same meeting room, and there were another 100 or 150 other guests there of different ethnic communities. The door was wide open. We wanted the public to know. We would not have used a public location such as the Hotel Bosna. There was a restaurant there where there were guests. There were waiters there, serving drinks, and they were from all ethnic communities. They were doing their job and waiting on other guests as well. What secrets? Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. We wanted Alija Delimustafic at that meeting. We requested his presence. I did so personally, so that people could tell him what they think. They were unable to directly communicate with him. The chiefs in the field, that is. I wanted him there so that people could speak to him face to face. Of course, he did not come, but there is no reason for it to be -- to see it as something secretive. I think he is in Sarajevo now, and he can confirm what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think what you said, and that is not recorded, that he received the minutes and that he held it in his hands and that you can guarantee that he is in Sarajevo, and he can either confirm or deny that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P527.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, apparently you sent this document. It is your dispatch sent from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 13th February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that? Is it your dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, was this a secret dispatch in any way, or did you follow the usual channels through the MUP communications centre of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the regular channels. The communications system as it existed. People of all ethnicities worked there. This was no secret. This is just a regular dispatch. There are no specific designations as to its secrecy in the right-hand corner at the top. I apologise, this dispatch was sent as all other dispatches were. This was a regular way to communicate within the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it was a public and open dispatch, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was received by those on duty in the respective police stations and centres. Of course, it wasn't Stojan Zupljanin who sat there awaiting it, but those in charge the communications. Whether that person was Muslim, Croat, or Serb, we could not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, any dispatch sent from the communications centre of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was always processed in such a way that a copy would remain in the MUP archives; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe this is an archive copy of the Federation MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 1D139 to the witness. It is tab 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a decision of the interior ministry in Sarajevo, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina ministry, that is. The date is 14 February 1992. Signed by Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By virtue of this decision, Mico Stanisic is being appointed to the duties and tasks of advisor in the minister of the interior cabinet. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If, as you say, Mr. Delimustafic had this -- had the minutes of the meeting of the Serb personnel in Banja Luka, and he was informed of it by you, and he was asked to come there by you. All this, in any case, preceded this decision of his to appoint Mico Stanisic as his advisor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why any insistence is placed upon the secrecy or alleged secrecy of that meeting. Mr. Delimustafic was well aware of it, and I sent a dispatch to all of the addressees you could see a minute ago, asking that all officials be informed of within the respective areas of their police stations and centres. I don't understand. There was nothing illegal or secretive about it. As for Mico Stanisic, there was a vacancy, and according to the distribution of personnel, this was supposed to be a Serb position, and he appointed Mico Stanisic as an associate to his office. There was nothing secretive or illegal about the whole thing. Why insist on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 23rd of March, 1992, passed its Law on the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called at the time. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the date or whether it was published in the "Official Gazette" on the 23rd of March. That I am positive of. They must have -- may have voted on it before that, perhaps a day or two before. First it had to be adopted by the Assembly, and then it could be published in the "Official Gazette", so as to come into force some eight days later. One could find it in the "Official Gazette" of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To illustrate the situation even further with the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would kindly ask that you be shown 1D118.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document contains information on abuse, illegalities, and manipulation by SDA and HDZ officials in the service of the B and H MUP State Security Service, dated March 1992. I won't go through the document itself, because, more or less, it reflects what we have commented upon, especially the abuse by Mr. Munir Alibabic as well as some other facts, including the fact that the assistant chief of the State Security Service, which, under the agreement, was supposed to be a Serb, such a person was never appointed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Yes, there was a problem with personnel. Man number 1 in the state security sector was a Croat Branko Kvesic. Person number two was supposed to be a Serb who would act as his deputy. He was supposed to be the operational chief of the State Security Service. A Serb was never appointed to that position. I think they even changed the structure or the job classifications by abolishing that post. Had a Serb been appointed as was part of the inter-party agreement, it would be that Serb in charge of all operations, in effect, being in charge of the State Security Service. The powers that be would not have that, and a person was never appointed to that position. I think Vlasko Nedjo [as interpreted], a career policeman, was supposed to be appointed. But once this became a problem among the parties in power, they simply abolished that post. He was simply never appointed, although he was supposed to have been. I think his name was Vlaski Nedjo, but please don't hold it against me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, it was obvious that the SDA and HDZ did not honour even the inter-party agreement they signed alongside the SDS. That is obvious, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that the parties came to realise that the police ministry was to play an important role in the creation of the future state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At some point in time the inter-party agreements as well as the laws regulating the work of the police were violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this problem was pointed out during sessions of the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 1D120. Page 2, please. So that we can see who was in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the members of the council for the protection of the constitutional order of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were Stepjan Kljuc; Dr. Miodrag Simovic; your minister, Alija Delimustafic; and Izet Muhamedagic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: She was the president of the council.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was the president, and she was the official chief of the council. She was in charge of controlling the legality of its work. I believe in her absence, it was Ejub Ganic who acted as her deputy. It was because on a number of occasions she froze her membership in the council, due to the visits of Princess Elizabeth accompanying her on her tour of certain monasteries, that is Princess Elizabeth Karadjordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We see that the deputy minister of the interior was also in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the meeting was held, the session was held.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't present, but Vitomir informed me. Yes, we did know about the session because the problems were acute relating to the work related to the work of the state security, and they reached a peak at that time. And so Vito as a representative of the ministry, or, rather, the Serbian people in the police force, attended the session, as well as Dr. - what was his name - Simovic, who was the vice-premier in charge of internal policy, and later on he was chief of police and chief of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir -- Mr. Mandic, the day before yesterday Ms. Korner showed you a document. It is P532. It's your interview, a public interview that you granted on the 28th of March, 1992. Do you remember that you commented on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember seeing that, seeing the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you confirmed when Ms. Korner asked you that you granted the interview, and you confirmed its contents, and that's why I'm using it here and now. Now, in that interview, on the 28th of March, 1992, you talked about everything that you and I discussed yesterday and today concerning the problems that existed in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth of it. Everything else is manipulation. All that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on page 1, you say: "In the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially over the last two or three months, during the last two or three months, the national police force of Muslim people has legally been established. After Hilmo Selimovic had resigned from the position of assistant in personnel section and the arrival of Mirsad Srebrenkovic from Zagreb some strange things ban happening, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this person was a religious teacher from the Mesihat. He didn't work in the mosque but in the Muslim Islamic school, the Mesihat, and you have a man like that coming to head a multi-national community in a multi-national state where officials were mostly the socialist officials and cadres who didn't know a lot about God and didn't believe in God much of any confession. And it was a shock for us, and I have to repeat that. It was a real shock. The meeting was interrupted for the man to go and pray. That was unprecedented as far as we were concerned. And that's why I referred to these secular Turkish state where you couldn't do that kind of thing, you can't do that now. And Iran, pro-Shiite introducing Islamic laws in state organs, well, that was the crux of the problem within the police force. And I, as a socialist official, never went to church. I didn't go to church at all, except maybe three times for a funeral or christening. And here have you this man coming in, interrupting the meeting at noon, and going off to pray. I can't describe to you in words how shocked I was, and what the situation was like. And our leading Muslim, Hilmo Selimovic, who lives and works in Sarajevo to this day, was in favour of secularism, was dismissed without any explanation or anything. So if somebody can explain to me why that was the case, then I might be able to accept it, but I just can't understand. And this happening in Europe? I could never envisage anything like that taking place in Europe. And half my friends were married to women of other ethnicities. My wife's a Catholic, and so on and so forth. And that was the general rule in Sarajevo, especially after the Olympic Games -- well, before the Olympic Games as well. And we were in Europe, and had none of this happened with the nationalist parties being victorious, pressing their national positions, and so on, none of this would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, you didn't mind, you weren't bothered by the fact that this man was of the Islamic faith. What did bother you was that he would do so in working hours, if I can -- during the working day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I have many friends who are Muslims in Sarajevo. I always have had and still do and will do. So that wasn't a problem. But it -- it was introducing these religious rights into a secular state. That was the problem. Otherwise you were free to follow your own faith. And those who had been to the police academy and were in the structures of power and authority within the polices force, what was happening was something that we just didn't understand. We just saw it on films when this man Khomeini returned to Iran, and things like that. That was a shock for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now in this document, sir, Mr. Mandic, you say, on page 1, when asked by the journalist, Does all this mean that there's no united MUP anymore? And you said: "That's right. There is no united MUP. That's a thing of the past. There hasn't been a united MUP since the days of -- well, since the time that 1400 people were employed working for the SDA and when 30 Serbs fled from Stari Grad," and so on and so forth. And you stand by that, still? Do you still maintain that that was the historical circumstance, that the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could no longer operate in the way it had been operating before that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was reality at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, in this document, in this interview, you state that it was your wish as a professional to have a united MUP persevere, but that it wasn't possible given the situation. And I'm going to show you your -- well, if we turn to page 2. It is rather a poor copy. It's been copied many times, but let me read it out: "If, as you say, a single or united MUP is the past, how, then, do you see the organisation of this institution in the future? Let politics decide. What the parties decide will be followed. If the Serb Assembly decides to form a Serbian MUP, then I agree with that."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were the people who carried out the decisions taken by the politicians, the parliaments, and the Assembly of the Serb people. And that was logical; it couldn't be otherwise. At least that is what I was taught when I studied at the faculty of law in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact remains, Mr. Mandic, and I think you said this yesterday during your conversation, or maybe two days ago, when Ms. Korner was questioning you, that it was your position within the frameworks of the MUP collegium of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you professionals, the professional staff, that you should do your work professionally and leave it to politics and politicians to decide and that you would behave in line with their decisions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, on the 23rd of March, 1992, in the "Official Gazette," the Law on The Ministry of Interior was published of the Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you confirmed that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, towards the end of that law, it's -- it is stipulated that the law comes into force eight days after having been published in the "Official Gazette".

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was customary, was it? That was the usual -- the usual practice and -- well, that was the deadline for a law to come into force, right, eight days after publication?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in conformity with that, on the 31st of March -- and that is P353. Tab 17. P353 is the document number. You sent this dispatch, the one you have before you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to repeat what it says here. We have looked at it several times, but this dispatch was sent to everybody within the Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this dispatch in the preamble, if can I call it that, says that it is pursuant to a Sarajevo Agreement on the Cutileiro Plan and the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into three entities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry that we don't have the original of Cutileiro's Plan here, but this dispatch reflects Cutileiro's Plan with respect to the partition of the police, and it says that the local police force should be based on the ethnic composition of the population in the area. So this dispatch in fact reflects certain portions of the Cutileiro Plan or, rather, the Sarajevo Agreement which was signed. And ultimately there was war and many crimes were committed, and people were killed, many people were killed, but the international mediators returned, and the parties returned -- or, rather, they went back to the Cutileiro Plan. And now we have the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the police as it is set out in this dispatch which was reasserted by the Dayton Agreement and the BH Constitution. So if we had stayed with the Cutileiro Plan and the agreement reached by the internationals and so on, there would have been no war. And you would have had the situation as it is today in BH in 1992. Now, Bosnia-Herzegovina would -- and Bosnia-Herzegovina would have become part of the international community even before the other countries. Look at the Dayton Accords, look at the Cutileiro Plan and this dispatch, as far as the police is concerned it is an exact copy. And what did we have in the mean time, a bloody war for four years. And who is responsible [realtime transcript read in error "espionage"] for that, I ask you? Just take a look at the facts. Dayton sanctioned this dispatch, and I'm referring to the police, of course, when I say that, and the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Serb police force still exists in Republika Srpska with these five districts where the district courts are in authority, where the prisons were set up, the district courts were set up, the misdemeanours court were set up, municipal courts were set up, and so on. I didn't think all this up. That's what the mediators thought up, and that is how it was. And the Serbian People's Assembly adopted a Law on Internal Affairs speaking about that and the -- or the Assembly passed that on the basis of the Cutileiro Plan and the Sarajevo Agreement, signed by the representatives of all three ethnic groups. And there should have never been a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would take a break now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to correct the -- Your Honours, can I -- it says at the moment -- the transcript reads at page 31, line 16, "a bloody war who is espionage for that I ask." I rather think that the word was "responsible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move too far away from the February 11th meeting, I inquired of Mr. Zecevic, whether he proposed to put to Mr. Mandic what his client asserted in interview to the OTP investigators way back whenever it was, 2004, I think, 5. Namely, that it was Mr. Mandic who scheduled the meeting that took place on the 11th of February and actually organised it. I don't know -- Mr. Zecevic thought that he had said that, but I've checked and I can't any see reference to it. Of course, we go back to the same problem. There is no obligation on the Defence to put a case, subject to what Your Honours may or may not rule in respect of our motion about this. But it seems to me that Mr. Mandic is here. He has been asked a lot about the 11th of February meeting. If that is still the Defence case, then that is a matter that Your Honours may feel that Mr. Mandic should be asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness said himself that he invited Minister Delimustafic to the meeting. He personally invited Minister Delimustafic to the meeting. And it is our understanding that he is doing that because he's organising the meeting. That is our understanding. But I'm perfectly willing to ask the witness, again, to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a slight difference. Saying that I asked Mr. Delimustafic to the meeting; it is not the same thing as, I personally organised the meeting and scheduled it in Banja Luka. That begs the question entirely. Because, I mean, he may have asked Mr. Delimustafic on the basis somebody said, Here, Momo, we're having a meeting of all the Serbs in the MUP. Do you want to come along? Which is not quite the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the significance that it may have to clarify who exactly organised the meeting, whether it was Mr. Mandic or somebody else, my simple question would be to Mr. Zecevic if would you mind actually clarifying this matter with the witness when he comes back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because if it is a point of contention, then we might as well clear it up while he is here. So if you would be so good as to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I understand, Your Honours, and I appreciate -- and of course, I will ask that. I didn't thought that that was an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, I hope that your dispatch dated 31 March is still before you. You explained to us all the background. And at the very beginning you told Ms. Korner and later on you told me how that dispatch came about, that it was drafted by your assistants and you. I would just like to -- to read out to you the last paragraph of your dispatch where you say that: "All staff who were" -- who had jobs with the MUP on that date would be taken over by the MUP of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you go on to say that these staff, before becoming officially employed, must make a solemn declaration. It's a fact, isn't it, Mr. Mandic, that Article 41 of the law states the words of the solemn declaration required to be given by every MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina and all of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, tell me, it was certainly not in your interest to cleanse the MUP of non-Serbs, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I stated in the dispatch. And I say that in the dispatch. There was no reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph you insist that all MUP staff of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina must be acquainted with the contents of the dispatch so that they may be objectively informed in a timely fashion so that unwanted situations be avoided; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will see later on that that this was also the position of the collegium. But I'm asking you as the author of this dispatch, its essence was that the MUP should be divided without problems peacefully and in a civilised manner?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we did, Mr. Zecevic. I think it was on a Tuesday or a Wednesday in early April, when at the professional collegium, we agreed - and I believe that everybody was present, only except for Mr. Delimustafic, he attend as cabinet meeting - we agreed that the MUP be divided in accordance with this dispatch and that, pursuant to the Cutileiro Plan, such a structure of the police be established as corresponds to the ethnic makeup of the then-regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was agreed upon. We discussed that. We made -- that's what we stated, and we reached that conclusion. I believe that two or three days later, a meeting was held of all the professional staff of the joint MUP, our objective being that everything be done peacefully and democratically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it is the Prosecution case in this trial that all these problems we have discussed so far from mid-1991 on in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the irregularities, all illegal acts that may have been committed, were merely a pretext for the Serb leadership to do what they had intended to do from the very beginning anyway; namely, to tear up Bosnia-Herzegovina and can carry out a joint criminal enterprise and ethnically cleanse Bosnia-Herzegovina from non -- or of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as you were one of the highest-ranking executives of the MUP, you were a long-standing police professional, after which you became a judge, and you're a lawyer by training. Tell me, please, whether the problems we have discussed were so great and so complex and so important, as you said in the interview you gave on the 28th of March, that, due to all that, a partition of the MUP was inevitable?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Due to that peaceful partition of the MUP, there has never been a confrontation of police forces of the individual ethnic groups, except at Vrace, where the Serb special police was ambushed. Pursuant to the orders given by Minister Delimustafic, the Serb special forces were relocated to Vrace and the Croatian special forces to Bjelovar. And it was due to that fact that there were no major armed clashes between members of the police who belonged to different ethnicities, nowhere, in no area. We only carried out orders, and politics was up to the politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now that we're talking about this, isn't your impression the same as mine; namely, that, the Serbs or the SDS, did not want war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they didn't. And I don't think the Muslim people or the Croat people wanted it either. The people didn't want war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We only wanted to live in our own state, to agree on things, and go toward Europe, especially after the Sarajevo Olympics, who could have wanted war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when I asked you about the inevitable partition of the MUP and the allegation of the Prosecutor, namely, that there was a plan in existence according to which the partition of the MUP was the trigger of all subsequent events. You were asked a similar question in the Krajisnik case and you answered in the negative. But could you now please elaborate a little. Do you still say that this is absolutely wrong?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once more. The minister's collegium in its first composition cooperated well. And we were kind of a buffer for the -- for the tall aspirations of the highest leadership. Nobody of us wanted the MUP to be divided. We were professionals. Politics played no role in that. And it isn't correct that my dispatch or the partition of the police triggered the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Other things triggered it, but they were outside of the police. From Minister Delimustafic to the police officer on the beat, nobody could have affected that or taken part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if I may, just a moment. We tried to prevent the creation of a militant Islamic malitia, not police, a militia in the framework of the police and under the cover, as it were, of the MUP. Hundreds of people came in, and they received badges and weapons. So we saw that a militia was being created, not a police. And within our police force -- Bosnia-Herzegovina is small. We got that information. And we, I mean the Serb [indiscernible] staff, tried to prevent that. If that was the cause of the war, well -- but I don't think it was. The cause of the war were other things that had nothing to do with the police or police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you saw militia, you basically mean this party militia, one single ethnic militia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, what a -- militia -- what a militia -- when I say militia. We know what a militia is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mandic. Immediately after you had sent out this dispatch to everybody in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the then-minister, Mr. Alija Delimustafic, sent out a dispatch, I believe, one minute after your fax was sent, the fax with his dispatch went out. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look at the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D136.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delimustafic -- I am sorry, Mr. Mandic; I apologise. In this dispatch, Mr. Delimustafic, about halfway down, says that he cannot elaborate on the regulations pointed out in your dispatch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot see where counsel is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this section?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know this dispatch by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll have to repeat. It's is halfway through the document in the Serbian language. The sentence starts about the contents of the dispatch in question, Taking into consideration all dilemmas, pointed out the dispatch, I cannot -- I'm unable to dwell more closely on -- et cetera, because they are unknown to any of the professional services in the MUP, nor were they presented to me by anyone, not even by the workers in charge whose names are mentioned in the dispatch? You say you saw that? I'm waiting for the transcript. You confirmed, sir, that you saw it, and that you're familiar with this dispatch. Mr. Mandic, it follows from this dispatch, let me put it this way, that the minister, Alija Delimustafic, was caught by surprise when he saw your dispatch and that this partition of the MUP and all that was a surprise to him, if I understood your testimony correctly these past two days. First of all, the Assistant Minister, Mr. Vitomir Zepinic --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Vitomir Zepinic, deputy minister, was appointed minister of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina which was published in the "Official Gazette" in January. Mr. Delimustafic must have known about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he knew, and we did all this in agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was, of course, familiar with the text in the "Official Gazette" which published the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was also familiar, because you said you provided him with the minutes of your meeting of the 11th of February, he was familiar with it as well. Following which, he appointed Mico Stanisic as his advisor. Hence, Mr. Delimustafic was completely familiar with it all, and you said a moment ago that you did this in cooperation with him.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this daily. We had offices one to the next in the same building, and the minister could always -- was always familiar with what I was discussing. He had all the information. He was probably the most and best informed person in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He knew everything that was going on inside the ministry and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain this dispatch of his, of the 31st of March then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had to follow the orders of his party. He had to honour their position, and he frequently said so. He couldn't prevent Srebrenkovic being appointed, although he was the chief of police. No one asked him. Otherwise he would have been removed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, this dispatch he sent was actually the results of the pressure exerted upon him by the SDA. For some reason, the SDA wanted to do this.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under the pretext that there should be a single police. Mr. Cengic who was in charge of that as well as Avdo Hebib, who was his advisor, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you said that it was done because the SDA wanted to form a single-party militia under the clout of the MUP as a whole; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, I think, in answer to Madam Korner's questions on day one of your testimony, that after this dispatch of the 31st of March, you sent out another in which you provided further explanation of the functioning of the joint MUP, which was supposed to take over some of the prerogatives belonging to the joint MUP. And in keeping with the Cutileiro Plan, the three entities should have their respective police forces in keeping with your dispatch. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We provided further explanation in that dispatch. We said that the police staff would be trained and educated in joint schools, and that certain services, such as logistics and those aiding operational -- the operational aspects should remain the same. This was simply a model we put forth on how to organise the police across the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'll show you a dispatch of 1 April. It is 1D78. This is a dispatch sent to all, to the minister, the federal SUP, all CSBs, all SJBs, much like your previous dispatch of 31 March. This is a -- the report or the minutes of the MUP collegium of the Socialist Republic of B and H held on 1 April 1992. You mentioned the collegium meeting a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the agreement. There was certainly no trigger. Everything was arranged at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can see here that reference is made of the Sarajevo Agreement in paragraph 1. It also states that the general provisions were confirmed yesterday during a meeting in Brussels on the important segment of state functions and that the reorganisation of the MUP is already under way across the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that it seemed to you that Mr. Alija Delimustafic did not attend that collegium meeting. However, in addition to deputy minister, Mr. Zepinic, there was also Mr. Branko Kvesic, HDZ representative; Mr. Jusuf Pusina; then Mr. Sabic; Avdo Hebib; and some others who were there on behalf of the SDA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collegium meet in its full composition together with the deputy minister from the minister's office. This was the full collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the document says what you have discussed a moment ago, i.e., what were to be the joint services, et cetera. On page 2, towards the middle, the collegium calls upon all to deal with the situation without excesses in a peaceful fashion so as to transform the existing MUP in its seat as well as in the field. It also says that there should be no one-sided firing of staff based on their ethnic background and that the employees should voluntarily decide on their further engagement and status. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was, indeed, the collegium's position.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same principle was followed when the Yugoslav republics went their own ways. People could choose where to live and work, and so here could choose which police force they were to join. The collegium insisted upon this. Everyone was there, save for the minister. All those community's representatives agreed upon that. This was our joint position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this dispatch, in the signature block states: Collegium of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this by chance, or was it intentional that the entire collegium is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was no chance. This was our joint position. The conclusions were such. All members of the collegium were present, save for Mr. Delimustafic. Mr. Zepinic stood in for him, as well as his two deputies, Hebib and Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, it was intentional that the dispatch was signed by the collective MUP collegium of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina so as to indicate its joint position.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The position that had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mandic, following this, the first subsequent thing done in keeping with the agreement was the division of the special unit of the Socialist Republic of B and H MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's put it in a context. It is a fact, is it not, that during the fall and towards the end of 1991 and in early 1992, there were certain problems with the use and engagement of the special unit of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of B and H?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Namely, that unit was used for searches of areas, for mistreatment of certain people, especially Serbs in the environs of Sarajevo and at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an anti-terrorist unit. The name speaks for itself. This is what it was supposed to be used for, against terrorists, sabotage, et cetera. In late 1991, however, it was used to search houses and apartments in the municipalities of Foca; in Bileca [phoen], in the settlement of Pofalici; in Sarajevo; and in Bosanski Brod. Those searches mainly concerned Serb houses. People in the field and deputies reacted to it, asking that the anti-terrorist unit not be used for things that would otherwise be done by the regular police. It was our agreement following these objections to meet at Krtelji in the seat of the special unit. We met with the commander and his assistants, whereby we agreed that the special unit could not be used without the approval of the tripartite leadership, that is to say, one member of each ethnic community. That was the decision that was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I read somewhere, or maybe you said it, that you were at the very meeting at Krtelji when this tripartite key was agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are minutes from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Mandic, isn't it true that Vitomir Zepinic, as deputy minister, received a task from Mr. Delimustafic, the minister, with the approval and support, so to say, of the collegium of the senior staff of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of B and H, to carry out the partition of the special forces along ethnic lines in early April.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think the Krtelji meeting was attended by Zepinic, as well as Jusuf Pusina and Bruno Stojic. They agreed then the Serb part of the special unit, that is to say members of Serb ethnicity, of whom there were 35, were to go to Vrace, to the former building of the special unit. The building was called TEF, T-E-F, and that they were to be accommodated there pending further political solutions and that the rest of unit should go to the police hall the Bjelovar settlement. Delimustafic confirmed as much in Sarajevo, that this had indeed taken place. Delimustafic issued an order to that effect, and the order was followed through. This was a peaceful dissolution or division into two different facilities, pending the political resolution on MUP partition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you mentioned Mr. Delimustafic. It is a fact, is it not, that Mr. Delimustafic, as you have just said, testified in a criminal proceedings against you before the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2007; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that Mr. Delimustafic in that case appeared as your Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
