utterances.text: And, as you have just said, Mr. Delimustafic confirmed all the facts about the MUP partition at your trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, we have the record of that trial.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe his words were quoted in the judgement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic, following the meeting at which, as you say, there were representatives of all three sides, that is to say, Mr. Zepinic, who was a Serb; Mr. Jusuf Pusina, a Muslim; and Mr. Bruno Stojic, a Croat. The decision on the partition was made --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The division or partition, so as to avoid any further conflict. These were special forces, trained people who had been stationed there for a while. And the Muslim personnel actually refused to go to Bosanski Brod. They refused to carry out any further searches of Serb houses. And then Mr. Delimustafic said that they did not want any armed conflicts within the police. Do send one part of the special force to the school of the interior and the other to the police hall at Bjelovar, which is close to the MUP seat. This was arranged, and it was done the same way, as requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me take you back for a moment to the beginning of April or, rather, that was the 1st of April. Now let's go back to the 1st of March 1992 when the killing took place at the wedding ceremony, the killing of the Serb member of the wedding party at Bascarsija. Now we heard claims saying that that was a political killing. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a policeman, so let me tell you. And I will describe it to you and tell you what happened. Within the nucleus of the old part of Sarajevo there is 12th, 13th century church, a Serbian Orthodox church dating back to the 12th or 13th century, and that part of Sarajevo is inhabited mostly by the Muslims, 99 per cent of the population are Muslims, in actual fact. And it is an Orthodox custom to go to church without any weapons. The father of the bride was carrying a Serb flag with the emblem of the double-headed eagle. And Delalic, a man who had a criminal file with a friend of his, whether he was irritated when he saw a Serbian flag flying through Muslim-inhabited area, killed him. And this caused a major problem. I was head of the crime department, and we learned who the perpetrator was very quickly and where the perpetrator was hiding. But we weren't able to go and arrest him and act according to the law, which we were duty-bound to do, because he was guarded by the reserve police of the Stari Grad police station led by Dahic. Sixty armed people with long rifles stood guard over him. Now the man's son, the man who was killed, his son came to see me and so did the clergyman, the Orthodox priest. And he asked me, he said, Mr. Mandic, among other things, how much money did you get, and what is it that the Muslims gave you to protect the killer, my father's killer? So this was an escalation of various misunderstandings. The Serbs took to the streets and blocked the whole of Sarajevo for 48 hours. And we didn't know what to do. We knew who the killer was; we knew where the killer was. We knew what we were supposed to do, and we just couldn't do it; we couldn't act. So anybody who wasn't in a situation like that doesn't know what it means, and I can't explain it to you. But we were completely impotent, helpless. We couldn't act according to our rules of service. If they had allowed us to arrest the man and keep him in prison if he was irritated by the flying of the Serb flag and if he was handed over to the investigating judge, the escalation would never have come about and Sarajevo wouldn't have been blocked for two days. The situation was highly tense and a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it's a fact, isn't it, that when the barricades were erected after that killing in Sarajevo, that the senior officials of MUP which was the joint MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, pursuant to a collegium decision, they want to the barricades to try and calm the people down and to try and solve the problem? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people had weapons in Sarajevo, all three ethnic groups. And they were at the barricades, all three ethnic groups. And for the space of 48 hours, nobody was wounded, nobody was killed, nobody was injured, and that was thanks to our operational work, mutual understanding, and the fact that we went to the barricades to try and calm the people down and prevent them from doing something stupid. And in the meantime the politicians sat down to negotiate, and the situation was resolved two hours [as interpreted] later. And I think today that it was thanks to the police, who, in a way, went to the places, toured the places, and patrolled the places where the people had gone out to the barricades, because, you see, you had you a Serb barricade on one side and Muslim on another and Croatian on another. Everybody was afraid of everybody else. And so we went to talk to the people; went up to the barricades; and nothing happened. No excessive incident happened within those 48 hours or two days. And in my opinion, that was an example of police success, that they were able to prevent anything bad from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the politicians resolved that in two hours, you meant two days, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 48 hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the substance of my question, Mr. Mandic, was this. What I was getting at was this: You on the other senior officials of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina went to those barricades on assignment, on police assignment, that was your duty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from -- on orders from Delimustafic, the minister, and on basis of an agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, Mr. Delimustafic confirmed that during the trial that took place in Sarajevo, that he gave you instructions to go to the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He even asked to us work 24 hours round the clock to prevent any outbreaks. The important thing was to calm the people down because they were so angry because the father-in-law of the bride had been killed in the wedding ceremony. So you can't explain to people that it wasn't just an extremist act and that this extremist act was a one off and didn't represent the entire Muslim people who, out of hatred and their propensity towards crime, carried that act out. Because one thing leads to another, you know. And it is difficult to explain something like that to the population. It was only us, we, who were able to go there and explain this to the people. And Muhamed Cengic, the prime minister, not the one now but the other one, Dukic, and Simovic, I think they went to the blockades, too, to talk to the people, to prevail upon the people. And they held meetings too. And we were able to resolve the situation quite quickly because the party heads were somewhere else, at some other meeting. They weren't in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all at the time. They were, I think, in Brussels or London or somewhere like that. Elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, it is the Prosecution case that the barricades were not erected spontaneously as the result of that killing, but that they were intentionally by the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is incorrect. It is 100 percent wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go back to April 1992. Mr. Mandic, you told us about Mr. Vitomir Zepinic and the reserves -- or, rather, the reservations that existed vis-a-vis his - how shall I put this? - well, his honour and decency bearing in mind the facts that were established that you told us about. You said that there were certain irregularities in his work and in his conduct. Now, Mr. Vitomir Zepinic on 4th of April, 1992, submitted his resignation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he tendered his resignation, the deputy minister of the police force, Mr. Vitomir Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document - it is P912 - now. That's the letter of resignation which Mr. Zepinic tendered on the 4th of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He sent this letter of resignation and signed it in the office of the President of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you were present when he did that, and what came before and after; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, Mr. Mandic, was there any - how shall I put this? - any conflict between Mr. Mico Stanisic and Mr. Vitomir Zepinic; and is it true and correct that Mr. Mico Stanisic pulled out a rifle and pointed it at Mr. Zepinic at -- in the office of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A pistol, interpreter's correction. A pistol, not rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you couldn't get into Mr. Krajisnik's office armed. Yes, there was a verbal dual and probably voices were raised, but he didn't attack him physically at all. As to this business about the pistol, there is no question of that. Nobody had any weapons on them; it was on the second floor of the Assembly, and the security service on the ground floor would keep your weapons. You couldn't enter with any weapons. They would search you. So nobody had weapons in Mr. Krajisnik's cabinet or offices. But that there was verbal dual, yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what was the verbal dual about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely the conduct of Mr. Zepinic and everything that happened around him. He was an intellectual, a highly capable man, but he involved himself in matters that did not concern him. And it was a difficult situation for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says here -- on page 50, line 17, that my question was that Mr. Stanisic took out a rifle and cocked it at Mr. Zepinic, but we were -- we talked about a pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Was a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I didn't notice that correction by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Mandic, that in addition to this whole situation and the fact that Mr. Vitomir Zepinic tendered his resignation that there was talk -- well, that there were discussions with Mr. Krajisnik that he offered Mr. Zepinic a post, a place, in the MUP of the Socialist or rather the Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were very close, Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Vitomir Zepinic. Well, it was a bit of an ugly situation, actually, because, after all, he was the number one man representing the Serbian people in the police force. And then when you're in a situation like that and there's some ugly things and undignified going on, on the one hand, and other hand, you have a staff and someone who is very intelligent and had many years in the police force, that is a very tricky situation, difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say ugly, ugly situation, are you thinking of the fact that Mr. Vitomir Zepinic was the top man in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was established that he behaved wrongly, in a undignified manner. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the following day, on the 5th of April, as we said, in keeping with an agreement reached and an order from the minister, Alija Delimustafic, part of the special units, the Serb members of the units, 35 of them, in keeping with the agreement, set out to the TEF facility at Vrace?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. On that day, the 4th of April, the special unit was divided. The Serb portion -- it was partitioned. The Serb portion went to a facility in Rakovica, and that's a settlement by the special's headquarters, because the facility they were supposed to go to was rather run down, nobody had used it for several years. And so we agreed or, rather, Mr. Zepinic and the minister agreed to clean the facility up, to carry out some construction work, prepare the facility so that part of the specials who were Serbs could take -- could go to the facility; whereas the other part of the specials unit made up of the Croatian and Muslim people went to the police Dom or centre, and that was in use. They had somewhere to go. It didn't need any refurbishment. So the Serb part sent the night in this catering establishment in Rakovica. And once the facility TEF had been put right, and it was within the compound of the police academy, they were able to take up residence there. And I think that Dr. Zepinic, might I add, whether he came to the Assembly from that meeting or went home in the meantime to have something to eat freshen up and then go to the Assembly, I don't know, but it was the day that the specials units were split in two, partitioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the letter of resignation by Mr. Zepinic that we just looked at, it had nothing to do with that division or partition or the partition of MUP. His resignation followed on as a consequence of the lack of dignity he had demonstrated in performing his functions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, when the members of the special unit arrived at the Vrace facility they were ambushed. And if I remember well, two were killed on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three were injured, and two were shot in the back of the head. There are documents in the case file against me in Sarajevo. So two were hit in the back of the head. They had set out for the third gate with their personal weapons. They had passed by the accommodation building for the students, and they arrived at the third building where the forensic facility was, and the accommodation facility where they were supposed to stay. And they were both hit in the -- or, rather, shot in the back of the head. One of them was Lizdek, and the other's name was Kupic. They had both completed a course and in -- at that centre at Vrace, there were 170 in all. I believe there are also medical documents to corroborate what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, that confrontation ended and that part of the special unit that consisted of Serbs found accommodation in the TEF building at Vrace; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, at the time you were assistant minister, and it was a Sunday; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Sunday, and the second day of Bajram; I remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On Monday and Tuesday, you went to work to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to your workplace; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was that those of us who had worked in the joint MUP should keep our workplaces until the new structure really started functioning. The new MUPs established under the Cutileiro Plan. And that we should assist in the establishment of these new MUPs. But Munir Alibabic devastated my office, and I came there two days -- on two days, but then I no longer went there because I understood that even my life was in jeopardy. Jusuf Pusina also recommended me not to come there any longer, and I didn't. Soon enough I was dismissed on the 8th of April by the joint cabinet when Jure Pelivan was prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So to sum up, the agreement was -- or the agreement that was reached, I suppose that happened in advance, but it was only verified by the collegium. And under that agreement, there certainly must have been a time-period for the transformation of the single MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina into entity MUPs pursuant to the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we were waiting for the politicians to find agreement so that we could -- we could implement that and start working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after that collegium session, the special police force was split, and there was a confrontation, a clash, but that was completed. But you still continued going to work, to assist in the further partition of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to do so. Let me just add that at Vrace, in that clash, two Serb special police forces were killed and two or three wounded, but none of those who ambushed them was either killed or injured. So the only victims were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then, on Wednesday, the 8th of April, you were dismissed from your position at the cabinet session; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, Delimustafic, if you have the document, actually dated my dismissal the 5th of April, although there was no cabinet session on that day. What's more, it was a Sunday and Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D00-0488. Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let's just wait for the English translation. Is this the dispatch about your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is dated 8 April, but as you said, the 5th of April figures in the text.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An earlier date is stated there. I kept going to work on the 6th and 7th. On the 8th, I was dismissed and no longer went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that the date when you were dismissed certainly is the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see that it was an urgent dispatch and which was sent out immediately after the decision of my dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there's opposition, I tend to -- I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit 1D256, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I think that Ms. Korner was assessing whether she would object.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... Can I [indiscernible] where this document comes from? I just want to ask. That's fine. No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It comes from disclosure; it has the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's fine. No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to pass on to another topic, so this may be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Agreed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before we continue with my cross -- with my examination-in-chief [as interpreted], let me ask you this. We just spoke about the 11th February meeting in Banja Luka. You confirmed that it was a public meeting and that you personally invited the minister, Mr. Delimustafic, to attend the meeting. It is my conclusion that you invited the Serb staff to join the meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I organised the meeting, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would the Trial Chamber want me to pursue this matter anymore, or you're satisfied?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's matter of the Chamber being satisfied. If you are the -- I don't know that we need to -- from my point of view, I don't think we need to explore the matter further. But at the end of the day, it is a matter for counsel, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, and I appreciate. I would just -- I was just trying to be of assistance. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, I will show you a document, which is 1D174. These are the conclusions of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of B and H from a session which lasted over four days, between the 4th and 8th of the month specified. Do you know there was such a Presidency meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please. I think we don't have the right page in the English -- yes, this is the right page now. And we need page 2 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 of this decision, signed by the President of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of B and H, Alija Izetbegovic, the date is the 4th of April, states: "A mobilisation should be carried out of the entire reserve force of the Socialist Republic of B and H police in keeping with the earlier decisions of the Presidency and government ..." In item 4 it says: "That in keeping with their own assessments, a mobilisation be carried out of civil protection units in the city of Sarajevo and in the municipalities in the republic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. This was the rump Presidency and the rump government, without any Serb representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'll show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P440.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which is a communique of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and its national security council. The date is the 4th of April, 1992, signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. In that very document, which is actually a public announcement marked urgent, he states that the rump Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina operating without any representatives of the Serb people has issued highly irresponsible and illegal instructions regarding the raising of Territorial Defence and people's self-organisation and the raising the civilian protection and reserve police. Do you recall this announcement signed by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 it says: "By inviting the people to self-organise, the rump Presidency has acknowledged the collapse of the constitutional and legal order as well as that of legal authorities and has thus instigated chaos, violence, and civil war." Do you agree with this assertion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "The Serb national security council invites the citizens to disregard the I ill-advised invitation of the rump B and H Presidency and do everything in its power to avoid civil war and the suffering of the people." Mr. Mandic, was this indeed the position of the SDS and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph Mr. Karadzic says should any Territorial Defence, civil protection, or reserve police units in any area respond to the invitation of the Presidency, Crisis Staffs in those areas should [sic] be activated," et cetera, et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It was tit for tat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tit for tat? You mean this was a reaction to the previous discussion of the rump Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this public announcement was yet another invitation, a call upon all to avoid a civil war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that is in keeping with what we have discussed a moment ago when you said that the Serbs truly did not want a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D175 shown to you. It is a document marked for identification. It is a dispatch of the minister of Defence, Mr. Jerko Doko, dated 5 April 1992. Among others, it was sent to the CSB and public security stations. The document is dated 5 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mandic, are you familiar with this dispatch by Mr. Jerko Doko, whereby he conveys the conclusions of the government on the call-up of the reserve force and TO units?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, in both versions, you can see that he conveys -- it is towards the middle of the page. The sentence begins, "It is tasked with ..." It says: "The interior ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina is tasked with securing appropriate weapons and equipment to TO units necessary to secure public law and order and protection of vital facilities and to instruct and coordinate the activities of TO bodies." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you pointed it out back in September in your documents. That is, September of 1991. Six or eight months before this, and we now see it being put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this actually happened. We tried to prevent any arming of any people, of -- of the police arming the TO. And who were they supposed to protect from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the next page of this document signed by Minister Jerko Doko --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 3. At the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence you see, I think it's on the following page in the English version, it is stated in this order by the minister of Defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- sorry, by that time it was Bosnia-Herzegovina. No, it was still the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 5th of April. It is stated: "TO units which will be mobilised to carry out the aforementioned tasks and under the provisions of the law aforementioned are subordinated to the police stations in the respective municipalities and should follow orders of the officials of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Mr. Mandic, it is not in dispute that you and the Serb personnel in the MUP countless times in 1991 and 1992 warned of this that the police was being turned into an armed force, or rather that a party militia was being constituted. And indeed, on 5th of April, this was put into practice by virtue of this order of the minister of defence. Your fears were justified as early as 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, given that the witness recognised and is familiar with this document and he confirms its contents, I propose that we remove the MFI designation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There doesn't seem to be any resistance from the Prosecution, so the -- so ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Next, could we please have 1D00 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, this document now is 1D175. Thank you. [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D00-4780.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is an urgent dispatch sent to the entire MUP of the Socialist Republic of B and H. The date is 6 April 1992. It says: "Immediately implement all three degrees, (I, II, and III) of the order on alert measures." Signed by the interior minister, Alija Delimustafic? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the number at the top, 08-8. It would seem that this number was used by one of the deputies of the minister, because the minister's number was 01.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. He was 01, and this was sent by someone from his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this dispatch? Do you recall the alert measures being raised?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D00-2282.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see that this is a dispatch by which the Doboj CSB chief, Andrija Bjelosevic responds to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the joint MUP, on the same date, the 6th of April, 1992, referring to the order we just saw, the dispatch that is, the number of which is 08-8 of 6 April 1992. In this dispatch, the centre chief points out to the ministry that the alert measures of the first and second degree are to be taken after the declaration of a state of emergency, and of the third degree once the declaration of a state of war took place which is in the jurisdiction of the SFRY Presidency, according to valid regulations. Next he says: "In addition, according to your document from November 1990, the MUP receives and transmits the ordered readiness measures but cannot order them." Are you familiar with this dispatch and position put forth by Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this dispatch, but I am familiar with this position, and I know that the first dispatch was illegal. I don't think Alija sent it at all. In any case, I don't know of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mandic, do you agree that Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic in his dispatch is conveying what is stipulated by law?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Ministry of the Interior can't proclaim states, states of anything, and that's what the Presidency does. The ministry implements it, and Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic explains here who does what very correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there are any objections from Ms. Korner. I can see there are. Then I won't even attempt to tender this document. Thank you. May Mr. Mandic be shown 1D00-4778 [realtime transcript read in error "1D00-4776"] next, please, in tab 13. It is another dispatch sent to the entire MUP of the Socialist Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's a mistake in the transcript. I said 1D00-4778. The last digit was 6 there. So it's 8. Maybe I misspoke, and if I did so, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Mandic, here we have the dispatch dated the 8th of April, 1992. And it refers to the dispatch from the Ministry of Defence which we looked at a moment ago, signed by Minister Jerko Doko. And this is an elaboration of that. It follows on from that order, an elaboration by the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it says, in paragraph 2: "Inform us of your progress in completing the resubordination of appropriate TO, Territorial Defence units to the competent organisational units of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including problems and lack of clarity in the completion of this operation." Now, paragraph 3, it goes on to say strict categories -- strict records must kept according to categories. Active police force is the first point. The second bullet point is active personnel out of uniform. Then reserve police force. Then under, 4, reserve personnel out of uniform. And then 5, TO members, Territorial Defence members, that is. And 6, volunteers or other men liable for military service placed under the command of the SJB. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this document actually covers everybody. All those who are in a position and capable of bearing arms, right, it refers to all of them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is signed by an O. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Osman Jasarevic. He was chief of a police administration within the MUP headquarters and a colleague of mine. We were in the same class or year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he worked in the -- yes, ministry of the Socialist Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a head of a police department. Osman Jasarevic, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now these facts, as set out here, once again confirm what we were saying earlier on and everything that you pointed out to us in 1991 and 1992. It was proved in practice in 1992 that all your fears and caution was justified. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Ms. Korner isn't looking at me, which means she has an objection. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I didn't know that there was an application to admit this. Sorry, are you asking for this to be admitted as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to round everything off, and the witness's statement and testimony, since the witness did not recognise the document, I would like it to be at least MFI'd. I don't want to tender it because I don't think we can do so, because the witness didn't actually recognise it. I don't know how the Prosecution feels about this, but perhaps MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like again if I could be told from where the document comes. I am afraid. Anyhow, for the moment, I certainly would object to it being admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will give you an explanation for this document. But certainly it's from the sources that I enumerated in my letter to you a few months ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I know that. But I need to know, there are sources and sources, and I have rooted -- or a root-and-branch objection to anything that comes from General Prlic's web site. So if is one of those, then I'm going to object to it even being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me assure that it is not a document from General Prlic's web site, or any other web site for that matter. It's just that I can't give you a specific explanation for this document, but I will do so in due course. But if I understood, Ms. Korner, I don't think she objects to having this document MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If only for the sake of moving on, we'll marked for identification at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D257, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd like to show you document 1D152 next, please. Which is the transcript of a Presidency session, BH Presidency session. And I would like to us have page 2 displayed, please. It relates to -- page 2, please. It relates to Mr. Avdo Hebib, whom we talked about. And you remember, I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 of the Serbian, please. Yes, and page 2 of the English as well. Thank you. Both the page 2s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You'll remember, I am sure, sir, that we commented your -- about your letter and the written caution that you sent with respect to Mr. Avdo Hebib, where you said that he dealt in arming and armaments and that nobody in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BH knew what he was engaged in, and that he caused problems, inter-ethnic problems, and that he was leading up -- helping to lead up to a civil war. I think that is what you said in respect of Avdo Hebib; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this transcript, of the Presidency meeting at which Minister Delimustafic was present, he says: "Both we and his ministry made mistakes. Like what Bakir or Avdo Hebib did," and in bracket it says, "(Assistant Minister for police) when he ordered the war to start, people to open fire, occupy the barracks. He sent the order to all centres without my knowledge. He declared war. I told him to issue a statement to observe the proper form. He never came to see me again; he does not speak to me." And then Izetbegovic says: "Who did that?" And Delimustafic's answer is: "Avdo Hebib." And Izetbegovic says: "What did he do?" And Delimustafic says: "He declared war on the army, four points, sign the dispatch." Izetbegovic: "In what capacity?" And Kljuc intervenes there and says: "We have finished recording. Don't record this." Now, do you know that Mr. Avdo Hebib in fact started the war, as Alija Delimustafic claims here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who started the war. But certainly contributed to the war in the initial stages in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With this kind of conduct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we've finished with that. Now, Mr. Mandic, on the 8th of April, after you were relieved of your duties, you explained that, for a time, you assisted, if I can use the word, at the request of Mico Stanisic, assisted people in the Ministry of Interior during the month of April. And then, sometime at the end of April, you learnt that you would be appointed to the post of minister for justice and administration, and that happened sometime in mid-May 1992. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, it's not contentious that you, as a judge, your recognition as a judge, that wasn't contrary to your desires to be minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right, I was a lawyer. So it wasn't alien to me, if Nikolic didn't come to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the prime minister, Mr. Djeric, proposed you for the post of minister of justice; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, that very soon you and Mr. Stanisic - how shall I put this? - I won't say clashed, but that you didn't see eye to eye with Djeric. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as our personal relations went, there were no conflicts. But there was a divergence in the way that different ministries functioned, and, of course, that shouldn't mean a personal conflict. There was, first of all, a misunderstanding or a divergence of views between Stanisic and Djeric. And soon after that, well, already in the autumn, in actual fact, just prior to the Zvornik Assembly, Stanisic and me were on one side, and Mr. Djeric and Biljana Plavsic on the other. But only when it came to work and the way in which the state was supposed to function, or the Republika Srpska entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's also a fact, is it not, that Mr. Djeric, as prime minister, sat throughout 1992 in what was called an expanded Presidency, which, in addition to three Presidency members, Karadzic, Plavsic, and Koljevic, there were Prime Minister Djeric and Assembly President Krajisnik. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Supreme Command to be. And as the prime minister, he was part of that body, ex officio, and he was the number three man in the armed forces -- in the Supreme Command, rather. Dr. Radovan Karadzic was -- then Ratko Mladic. And the third man was Professor Dr. Djeric, Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I hope which agree that, as member of the expanded Presidency, where Dr. Djeric was at the source of all information, all available information; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, sometime in May, Mr. Trbojevic was appointed vice-premier; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic as vice-premier was in charge of the Ministry of the Interior departments and the Ministry of Justice departments.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was vice-president for internal policy, or, rather, he was the immediate -- my immediate superior. Mine and Stanisic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, even though he was your immediate superior, and Stanisic's too, at one point in time he sort of grew closer to the positions advocated by Prime Minister Djeric in this divergence of views and the clashes between Mr. Djeric and you and Mico Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Well, Mr. Trbojevic didn't like to be too prominent in any of these discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, Mr. Mandic, is it not, that the only two ministries which were really very serious about -- or worked seriously during 1992 and succeeded in achieving something, however limited, was the Ministry of Justice that you headed, and the Ministry of Interior, led by Mr. Mico Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in an official report of the work of the government in October at the Assembly in Banja Luka, Mr. Djeric, Branko Djeric, put the Ministry of Justice first when he boasted about the ministry and said that it had scored the best results by organising the justice system and regular courts, prosecutor's offices, and correction facilities, and my endeavours to unite the justice system, civilian and military. And there's a written report about that. In second place was the police, which tried to establish public law and order and under combat under the command of the army. And in combat -- of the army. So Mr. Djeric spoke about that and wrote it all down in his written report. And there's written trace of that because it is a written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said -- when you say the police, you meant the Ministry of the Interior; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ministry of the police, the Ministry of Interior, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you said in combat action when they were under the command of the army; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When there was an immediate threat of war, or -- and if there was fighting, then pursuant to the commander, the police had to be resubordinated to the army. That was under the constitution and the Law on Ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'll show you 1D96, which is the operational programme of the government called operational programme of measures to prevent disturbances to the functioning of the society under conditions of war. The date is the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This programme was put into effect by the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 2 in both versions. Could we scroll down so that the witness could see the whole page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm quite certain you're familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I won't go through the whole of it, since it's already an exhibit. Let me ask you this: It is not in dispute, is it, Mr. Mandic, that everything contained in this operative programme of the government that was under the remit of the Ministry of Justice is something you implemented.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were the only ministry which implemented all of the measures under the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The same goes for the Ministry of the Interior, more or less, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As Mr. Djeric specified in his report, the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All of the other ministries, due to objective or subjective reasons, or because of the situation, did not carry out even the basic of measures envisaged by this programme; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you - and when I say "you," I mean the justice ministry - managed, under wartime circumstances, to create a functioning ministry, establish courts, prosecutor's offices, prisons, detention facilities, from grass-root level; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was appointed justice minister, I had nothing, not even an office or a driver or a secretary. No paper, no pencils. Nothing. I worked 16 hours per day to establish the judicial system in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By the end of 1992, which is something I don't think is in dispute, the judicial system, following the October elections, began working, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it still works on the same principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you mentioned on a number of occasions that it was your position, as well as that of the ministry and of the senior leadership, was to respect the ethnic makeup on the ground, applied to those employed in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I am interpreting it well, it means that a certain number of non-Serbs - that is to say, Muslims, Croats, and others living in that area - were appointed as prosecutors and judges and to various positions within the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although there was must resistance in certain Assembly sessions by deputies. Despite of that, we managed to secure ethnic representation at all levels of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know by heart how many persons of Muslim ethnicity did you appoint to the positions of judges and prosecutors during your tenure in the ministry of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were 27 in the first wave, and we continued working on it. I think that was the figure, although I'm not 100 per cent certain. In any case, all those names can be found in the "Official Gazette". You can check it against that, who was appointed and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document shown to you previously by Madam Korner, which is P1333, which is tab 202. I think it was on the second day of your examination-in-chief that this document was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is definitely not it. This is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It came from your ministry. It is an overview of courts and prosecutor's offices number of elected judges and appointed public prosecutors in Republika Srpska. As it says, this is annex 1. I suppose it was an annex to your annual report of the Ministry of Justice. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At page two, we see that there was a total of 276 judges who were elected in 1992, in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please. I see that in the English translation the figure is missing. It says total of judges on the Supreme Court and then number 6. And just below that, it should be total, 276. In the English version for some reason it was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is stated there that the total number of prosecutors appointed was 80. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this tally with what you can recall? Do you have any reason not to trust these documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. This is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the next page, page 4, which is Annex 2 to your annual report, I presume, we see an overview of normative activity of Ministry of Justice and administration. We can see that your ministry worked on amendment proposals, laws, decrees, decisions, totalling 25 acts such as laws, decisions, decrees, and amendments. In that process, it also prepared another five pieces of legislation which were put up for discussion by the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we look at all this, Mr. Mandic, it is difficult to understand why Mr. Djeric, as far back as May, and then in August, and then in the fall of 1992, insisted on the reconstruction of the government, specifically pointing you and Mr. Stanisic out. Do you agree with me that this was illogical, especially having in mind the report he submitted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he specifically mentioned me and Stanisic in May and that fall. Is there such a document? Up to now, I had no knowledge of this. As for November and the Assembly in Zvornik, I have an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'll show you P190, which is a letter by Mico Stanisic sent to the Prime Minister, Branko Djeric. The date is the 18th of July, 1992. In it, puts forth a critique at the expense of Mr. Djeric. He states: "Although I'm a member of the government, I requested a number of times at governmental sessions that a draft law be created in keeping with international law and the laws of war, so as to direct the activities of the army, groups, and individuals," et cetera, et cetera. "You did nothing up to date, although I believe this was supposed to have been discussed on the first government session." Did you know that Mr. Stanisic sent this letter to Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there was a clash between the two of them, but it was the position which I supported that the paramilitary formations which came to the Bosnia-Herzegovina theatre were not to be allowed to enter the territory of Republika Srpska. He mentioned that a few times at government sessions, as you can see in the minutes. He insisted this area in particular be regulated by governmental decisions and laws. But this was not a clash. It was simply the position of a police minister who wouldn't have any paramilitary formations. I must tell that you they did a lot of -- they caused a lot of trouble. They robbed, first, non-Serb families. And when they ran out of those, they started robbing Serb families. And this is what the minister of the interior pointed out. I supported him in that. Mr. Djeric followed instructions of Madam Plavsic. She said at the Assembly meeting in Zvornik -- and there is a recording of it, as well as the minutes shown to me by Ms. Korner. On that occasion she clearly said: "I invited Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his Tigers. I invited the White Eagles. I invited some other animals and beasts, I can't recall who. And it is our minister, Stanisic, detaining them, preventing our brothers from abroad to help the Serb cause. He seems to enjoy Momcilo Mandic's position, and they are against other Serbs assisting us." My Defence counsel Milan Vujin used that footage. When Ms. Korner asked me about Mr. Stanisic, I said that we -- I said that he said to Ms. Plavsic that we allowed criminals to come in. She felt in need to respond, and she did so in Zvornik on 24th November. Mr. Djeric supported Ms. Plavsic on that. I remember well -- bare with me. I think there were some "Zuta Osa" or Yellow Wasps in Zvornik whom the police detained. And then Biljana Plavsic ordered their release. And of course there was a clash in the functioning of the authorities and the state. These were vein people, university professors. And it was my personal opinion, although I do not wish to insult anyone, they did not realise what it means that for some people who went unchecked to go into villages, robbing, and killing people and children. It seemed important to them to pose -- to have photographs taken with them, but as for the rest of what was happening, we disagreed strongly. Ms. Plavsic took this personally, and this is the cause of that rift or argument. Djeric, however, was on Ms. Plavsic's side. Please do show us the minutes of that session where she says, I invited them. She was a member of the Presidency and the Supreme Command. And there you have a minister who said, Well, you can't do that. She was insulted by that. And there was me, the minister of justice, seconding what my colleague said. Mico Stanisic, as the chief of police, said this a number of times to Djeric, President, we cannot control groups coming from all over into Republika Srpska. They kill children, they torch, rob, kill, and go back. They are these so-called weekend warriors, and they are officially supported by Biljana Plavsic. She appears on TV saying our brethren are coming to help us. They kill children, creating problems for everyone. Robbing people. And then we said, President, this cannot go on any longer. You are in charge of the state and of the police as well. And then Djeric resigned. He singled out me and Stanisic, and he said I had ties with Karadzic, and yet I wouldn't exchange a word with Karadzic for half a year because he allowed Plavsic and others to do this. I had my position. I spent my whole career in state bodies; I know how things work. They simply would not leave us room to do this. We wanted the judiciary; we wanted to people for certain crimes; and we wanted to prevent the entry of those paramilitary groups. They would arrive on a Friday; do all sorts of harm; and go back on a Monday. And then they say, Yes, this is how it should be done. And we said, President, this cannot go on. This is a shame for the Serb people. I was present when information came in of those people robbing Serbs and their property because there were no Muslims left any longer. It was me and Stanisic. We all knew about that. If this is exactly the -- the argument you have in mind. Branko Djeric was a member of the Supreme Command. He attended sessions of the Security Council, I think, comprised of professors, Plavsic, Djeric, et cetera. They thought we were their teaching assistants or students who were there to serve coffee. If you don't something they want you to do, there's trouble. And once you point out to them, Well, we're not to do this because Europe will never forgive us, then they think you're -- you've turned against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now let's take a look at page 2 of this same document, the same letter from Mr. Stanisic to Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please. It's page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see the sentence that is underlined there. It says -- Mr. Mico Stanisic says, and he is informing the prime minister: "We are working on collecting information and documentation of war crimes, i.e., genocide, regardless of who the perpetrators are and what their ethnicity is." And then he ends by saying: "Due to the potential responsibility that may emerge as a result of your insufficient involvement of this issue, I shall send this letter to you personally; to the Presidency of the Serbian republic of BH; as well as to the federal republic of Yugoslav SUP, secretariat of the interior, where a committee with one of our members is working on these very issues." And underneath there we have Mico Stanisic's signature. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is his signature. I am aware of this document. I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that was the position taken by Mr. Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we kept repeating that again and again and held debates on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this position taken by Mr. Stanisic, to the best of your knowledge, was implemented from the very beginning. And I'd like to show 1D61 to show you that, to see if you're familiar with the document. The date is the 15th of April, 1992. Do you see the document? It's an order signed by Mico Stanisic. And at the time, you were still helping out, if I can put it that way, in the MUP of Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already took over the Ministry of Justice, and I sent a similar dispatch before there, a fortnight before, the police station. And I think we discussed that document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think the date here is the 15th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I apologise, I was thinking of May. You're quite right. I was in the police then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree that it is very similar to the order we looked at a few days ago signed by you, the contents of which are almost the same. And that's what I want to ask you. So that was the position taken by the Ministry of Interior from the very outset; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were both policemen. We protected law and order, and life and property. We are just doing our jobs. So it is nothing unusual; it was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could the witness be shown 65 ter document -- no I apologise, P427; and .8, item 8 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is information from the -- or a report from the Ministry of the Interior. It says report on certain aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead, dated the 17th of July, 1992. Sent to the President of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic, and the prime minister. Do you see this report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I can't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and refresh your memory. Perhaps you know about some of the things contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to page 4, please. [In English] It's tab 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of July, 1992, Mr. Stanisic is informing the president, President Karadzic, and the prime minister of some phenomena on the ground that he was informed of at the collegium held on the 11th of July, the MUP collegium of Republika Srpska held in Belgrade. And he says: "The army and the Crisis Staffs" -- or, rather, War Presidencies are asking that the army collect or capture as many Muslims as possible and such undefined camps be left to the Ministry of Interior. The conditions there are bad, individuals not respecting international norms of conduct, and so on. Now, this report, is it not in keeping with what your knowledge was of the situation in July 1992, when you received information of this kind; and is it not in keeping with the instructions that we -- set of instructions that we looked at about captured persons and the authority that the army had over these individuals; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we show page 7 to the witness, please. Or, rather, page 8. May we turn to page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It reads, the first paragraph on that page: "The minister underlined the resolve that in order to achieve full legality constitutionality as well as the implementation of bylaws to do everything possible to prevent crimes from taking place, not only on the part of citizens but on the part of soldiers and army officers, the active and reserve policemen, members of the interior -- Ministry of Interior, and their officers for which it is established that they had committed crimes of any kind." Now it is true, that what is says there absolutely coincides with what you said earlier on, that, from the very beginning, that was the policy pursued by the ministry because you and Mr. Stanisic, as professional members of the Ministry of the Interior, could not act otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now on the next page, page number 10, it says the following. On page 10, one of the tasks mentioned is to prevent and document information about crimes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel give a specific reference, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that? About war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the next page. I think it's page 12, mentioning --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says -- it discusses the problems and states that one of the problems is the investigative centres, prisons, and collection centres that are in existence, and, in that regard, the responsibility of the organs, the MUP, so that the MUP in keeping with the law on Criminal Procedure and the Law on the Interior, on Internal Affairs, in order to carry out duties should act, vis-a-vis people, up to their trial and hand them over to the law enforcement organs; and specific discussion should be how to deal with the relocation of certain citizens, villages, et cetera, because this does not fall within the competence of the MUP, although efforts are being made to link it to the MUP. Now, do you know that Mr. Stanisic complained of problems of this kind and occurrences of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, I have five or six more documents to go through, and that will take me between 20 minutes and half an hour at the most. But as it is another area, I suggest that we adjourn for the day and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would reconvene in this courtroom at 10.00 -- 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just say one thing about the form of cross-examination. I haven't objected all morning, but I do think that cross-examination does require a question and not a comment such as, Now it is true that what is says there absolutely coincides with what you said earlier, that from the very beginning that was the policy pursued by the ministry, because you and Mr. Stanisic as professional members of the Ministry of Interior could not act otherwise. There isn't even the beginnings of a question there, Your Honours. I think questions should be questions, and not comments. And as I said, I haven't objected all morning, but just for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't want to -- because the witness already gave his answer to the previous question where he basically answered my question in anticipation what would be my question. That -- that is why I tried to summarise, just to save the time. But I'm perfectly willing to ask the witness, any time, Your Honour, his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.
